summary: Grade 4 learners (ages 9–10) solve multi-step measurement word problems — distance, time, capacity, mass, money — using the four operations on quantities that are often fractions or decimals. The core skill is MODELLING, not bare arithmetic: read the situation, build a visual representation (number line or bar/strip diagram) that captures the relationships, convert mixed units to a common unit, sequence the operations, label units and money symbols, check the answer is reasonable, and transfer the approach when a quantity changes. The habit to refuse is keyword plucking ('altogether means add'); learners who design their own representation before computing are the target.
misconceptions: Keyword plucking — grabbing the numbers and applying the operation a keyword cues, with no model of the situation
Operating across mixed units without converting (adding 0.75 m and 95 cm as if the same unit)
Treating time as base-ten (handling 1 hr 45 min as 1.45; carrying at 100 rather than 60)
Misaligning decimal points or dropping/mixing the money symbol (writing $5.7, or $0.50¢)
Computing with no diagram or estimate, so an unreasonable answer goes unchecked

activities.title: Build the model before you compute
steps: Read a multi-step measurement problem, e.g. 'A 2.5 kg bag of flour is shared equally into 4 tubs, then 150 g is taken from one tub — how much is left in that tub?'
Before writing any equation, draw a bar/strip diagram or number line that shows the quantities and how they relate (the whole 2.5 kg, the 4 equal parts, the 150 g removed)
Convert to a common unit where needed (150 g = 0.15 kg, or 2.5 kg = 2500 g) and note the conversion explicitly

Let the structure of your diagram tell you the operations: splitting the bar into 4 equal parts IS the ÷4 (each part = 2500 g ÷ 4 = 625 g = 0.625 kg), and marking off 150 g from one part IS the subtraction (625 g − 150 g = 475 g = 0.475 kg). Working in grams keeps the numbers whole, because 0.625 kg is in thousandths and Grade 4 decimal work usually stops at hundredths.
Estimate roughly first, then check the computed answer against that estimate and label the unit

Test transfer: if the same bag had been 3 kg instead of 2.5 kg shared into 4 tubs, predict whether each tub holds more or less and by how much before computing — the same partition-then-subtract model still applies
activities.insight: The diagram generates the operations, so you never have to guess an operation from a keyword; partitioning a bar is division and marking off a segment is subtraction. Checking against an estimate catches off-scale answers, and the same model transfers when a quantity changes (e.g. a 3 kg bag still partitions into four equal parts).

activities.title: Convert units before operating
steps: Given quantities in mixed units (e.g. 0.75 m, 1.2 m and 0.95 m; or 95 cm alongside 0.75 m), identify that they cannot be combined until expressed in one unit
Use a conversion table within a system (km/m/cm, kg/g, l/ml, hr/min) to rewrite every quantity in a common unit (95 cm → 0.95 m)
Only then add, subtract, multiply or divide, and label the result with the correct unit
Treat time carefully: 1 hr 45 min is NOT 1.45; minutes carry at 60, not 100 (e.g. leaving 09:20 and travelling 1 hr 45 min arrives at 11:05)
activities.insight: Operations are only valid between quantities expressed in the same unit; converting first prevents combining unlike units, and time is base-60, not base-10.

activities.title: Self-monitor and compare strategies
steps: At the start, ask yourself 'What is the problem asking?' and restate the goal before choosing a representation
After solving, ask 'Does my answer make sense?' and compare it to your up-front estimate
Solve a problem, then view or discuss an alternative strategy for the same problem (e.g. a bar model vs. a number-line path) and explain how each maps to the same operations
Explore a worked example where each diagram segment is annotated with the quantity it stands for and the operation the structure implies — use this for reference, then build your own on a new problem
activities.insight: Monitoring your own steps and comparing different valid representations can deepen understanding of why the operations follow from the situation, rather than from a cue word.

checkQuestion: Give the child two multi-step measurement problems that mix units and involve a fraction or decimal — e.g. 'A 2.5 kg bag of flour is shared equally into 4 tubs; then 150 g is taken from one tub. How much is left in that tub?' Say: 'Show your thinking with a diagram, then solve it.' Provide blank paper and watch: do they draw a number line or bar that models the situation BEFORE calculating, do they convert kg and g to a common unit, and do they check the answer is reasonable?
checkAnswer: Draws a representation (bar or number line) that captures the relationships, converts to a common unit (2.5 kg = 2500 g, or 150 g = 0.15 kg), applies the operations in the right sequence (÷4 then subtract), labels the answer with its unit, and can say why the size of the answer is reasonable.
